paper.title: Micro versus Macro Labor Supply Elasticities: The Role of Dynamic Returns to Effort
paper.code_data_availability: Henrik Kleven, Claus Kreiner, Kristian Larsen, and Jakob Søgaard. …

registers.role: outcomes / treatment / controls / linkage / sample frame

registers.name_in_paper: employer-employee matched data with DISCO occupation codes (DISCO-08 since 2010 with 563 occupations; DISCO-88 for 1991-2009 with 372 occupations; an older Danish classification with 299 occupations before 1991, bridged using a crosswalk from Humlum 2021)
registers.role: treatment (job cells and job switches: firm x occupation), linkage of workers to firms

registers.name_in_paper: mandated pension scheme Arbejdsmarkedets Tillaegspension (ATP) hours measure
registers.role: outcomes and controls (hours worked; binned measure, capped at full time for all 12 months)
variables_mentioned: annual hours worked (sum of monthly hours in four bins, 37 annual hours bins)

registers.name_in_paper: second administrative measure of hours worked (uncapped, monthly, all workers)
registers.role: outcomes (hours worked, used where hours variation must be captured precisely, including among full-time workers)

registers.name_in_paper: school grades (GPA for the highest education degree obtained by age 21, typically high-school GPA)

linkages: several administrative registers linked at the individual level via personal identification numbers
workers linked to firms through employer-employee matched data, defining jobs as firm x occupation cells
promoted workers matched to their unpromoted coworkers within the same firm, with the same event time

sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (person-quarter in the promotion event study; a balanced panel of persons observed every year from age 20 to age 50 in the descriptive analysis)
selection_rules: Baseline quasi-experimental sample: all taxpayers with baseline taxable income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK
Treatment status assigned by baseline (pre-reform) taxable income relative to a threshold at about the seventieth percentile of the income distribution
All switches are dropped where more than 50 percent of an individual's coworkers move to the same job cell in the same year (to avoid attributing reclassifications to job switches)
Descriptive analysis: a balanced panel of workers observed every year between the ages of 20 and 50
Promotion event study: individuals required to stay in the same firm from two quarters before promotion to two quarters after promotion

Mass-layoff sample: firm switches in which the original firm reduced its workforce by at least 30 percent and had a workforce of at least 20 employees (about one-fifth of job switchers in the baseline sample)
Donut specifications drop observations within +/-2.5 percent (small donut) or +/-5.0 percent (large donut) of the treatment threshold
sample.n_observations: 2,501,126 in the two-year elasticity regressions and 2,428,411 in the four-year elasticity regressions (Table 1, p. 2881); no N is printed for Tables 2 and 3 or for any figure

construction_notes: The outcome z_i equals total labor compensation, including contributions to employer-administrated retirement savings plans, so estimates are not influenced by shifting between taxable compensation and tax-deferred retirement savings contributions
The measure of taxable income that determines treatment status includes labor income, transfers, pensions, alimony, and certain capital income items
Jobs are defined as firm x occupation cells; occupation codes are bridged across DISCO-08, DISCO-88 and the pre-1991 Danish classification using a crosswalk developed by Humlum (2021)
Promotion is defined as a switch to an occupation cell in which median earnings are at least 10 percent higher (5 and 20 percent thresholds stated to be robust)

Delta log(1 - tau) is instrumented by a simulated mechanical tax change that accounts for changes in the tax code while holding individual income choices fixed at baseline values (Gruber and Saez 2002)
Pre-reform (placebo) specification: earnings growth 2006-2008 by 2006 income bin; post-reform specification: earnings growth 2008-2010 (and later) by 2008 income bin

The ATP hours measure: the annual pension contribution depends on annual hours, with monthly hours divided into four bins, giving 37 annual hours bins; the measure is capped at full time for all 12 months

The 2009 reform reduced the average marginal tax rate by 11.43 percentage points above the threshold and 1.70 percentage points below it, a difference in tax treatment of 9.73 percentage points; the marginal net-of-tax rate rose by about 17 log points over most of the treated interval and by about another 20 log points around the 350,000-400,000 DKK range

Panel B elasticities in Table 1 are obtained by scaling the switcher elasticities of Panel A by the cumulated fraction of workers who have made a post-reform job switch (equation 7), i.e. imputing a zero elasticity to job stayers

claims.statement: Among job switchers, the elasticity of earnings with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate is about 0.5 over a two-year horizon, which the paper interprets as the long-run (macro) elasticity.

treatment.label: Δlog(1 − τ_it) × D_it^Mover — log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate for job movers

definition.value: The log change in the individual's marginal net-of-tax rate, Δlog(1 − τ_it), interacted with a dummy D_it^Mover for moving between firm × occupation cells after the reform; estimated by 2SLS using simulated mechanical tax changes Δlog(1 − τ_it^sim) as the instrument (Gruber-Saez), which account for changes in the tax code but hold individual income choices fixed at baseline values. Identifying variation comes from the 2009 Danish tax reform, which eliminated the middle bracket and raised the top-bracket threshold, cutting the marginal tax rate by 11.43 percentage points above a treatment threshold at about the seventieth percentile of the income distribution and by 1.70 percentage points below it.

timing.value: Change between the baseline (pre-reform) year 2008 and 2010 for the two-year horizon and 2012 for the four-year horizon, with a 2006–2008 placebo window; treatment status assigned by baseline taxable income bin.

outcome.label: Δlog z_it — log change in total labor compensation

definition.value: Log change in z_i, total labor compensation, including contributions to employer-administrated retirement savings plans (so that estimates are not influenced by shifting between taxable compensation and tax-deferred retirement savings contributions); measured over a two-year (2008–2010) or four-year (2008–2012) window against the 2006–2008 placebo window.

timing.value: Two-year or four-year change relative to the pre-reform baseline year.

units.value: elasticity of total labor compensation with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate (1 − τ)

magnitude.interpretation: 'The structural earnings elasticity obtained from 2SLS estimation equals 0.486 after two years and 0.487 after four years' (p. 2881); the abstract calls the long-run elasticity 'around 0.5'.

estimand.target_population: job movers (firm × occupation switchers) treated by the 2009 reform; interpreted by the authors as point identifying the long-run elasticity in the population
estimand.time_horizon: two-year effect: earnings growth between 2008 and 2010, relative to the 2006–2008 placebo window
estimand.formal_query: ε = d log z / d log(1 − τ) for job movers (equation 25), interpreted as the long-run structural elasticity η

population.description: Danish taxpayers with baseline taxable income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK around the 2009 tax reform, with treatment status assigned by baseline taxable income relative to a threshold at about the seventieth percentile of the income distribution; the elasticity is estimated on job movers (workers switching between firm × occupation cells) relative to job stayers.
subgroups_defined: job movers (switchers between firm × occupation cells) versus job stayers
all switchers versus switchers in the top 10 percent of the income distribution
occupation switches, firm switches, and mass-layoff firm switches
population.selection: Treatment status assigned by baseline (pre-reform) taxable income bin; the estimation sample is restricted to taxpayers with baseline taxable income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK, and the elasticity of interest conditions on making a post-reform firm × occupation switch.

identification.source_of_variation: The 2009–2010 Danish tax reform, which eliminated the middle tax bracket and raised the top-bracket threshold, cutting the marginal tax rate by 11.43 percentage points on average above a treatment threshold located at around the seventieth percentile of the income distribution and by 1.70 percentage points below it (a difference in tax treatment of 9.73 percentage points), combined with variation in job switching between firm × occupation cells.
identification.instrument: Δlog(1 − τ_it^sim), the simulated mechanical change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate holding individual income choices fixed at baseline values (Gruber and Saez 2002)

key_assumptions.assumption: Quadruple-differences assumption: job stayers cannot respond to taxes, so non-tax differences in earnings growth above versus below the treatment threshold may change over time as long as they change in the same way for movers and stayers.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo (pre-reform) estimates are close to zero in the year-by-year profile (Figure 7); the 2006–2008 placebo series tracks the 2008–2010 series below the treatment threshold (Figure 6).

formal.as_written: γ_b − γ_b^P for stayers and β_b + γ_b − (β_b^P + γ_b^P) for movers; preferred estimates based on β_b − β_b^P

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: the simulated mechanical change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate predicts the actual change.
key_assumptions.supported_by: First-stage coefficient 0.486 with F-statistic 16,482.7 (two-year) and 0.441 with F-statistic 14,133.6 (four-year), Table 1 Panel A.

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: the simulated mechanical tax change affects earnings growth only through the actual marginal net-of-tax rate, because it holds individual income choices fixed at baseline values.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the simulated instrument as removing reverse causality from the endogenous choice of earnings in a progressive schedule, but states no separate test of the exclusion restriction.

key_assumptions.assumption: The timing of job switching is not selected on the underlying structural elasticity η (orthogonality between structural elasticities η and switching probabilities λ), which is what allows the switcher elasticity to point identify the long-run elasticity in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Flat time profile of mover estimates (Figure 7); bounds on selection bias from tax-induced switching (Figure 9); no effects of the reform on switcher characteristics (Supplemental Appendix Figure A.6); similar responses among mass-layoff switchers (Figure 10 and Table 2).

formal.as_written: E[ε_zt | J_t = 1] = s_t · η^T + (1 − s_t) · η^N

key_assumptions.assumption: Mean reversion: individuals with high pre-reform income are selected on positive transitory shocks, an unobserved common cause of baseline income bin and subsequent earnings growth that the design must net out.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pre-reform (placebo) regressions on 2006–2008 earnings growth by 2006 income bin; the quadruple-differences specification nets out stayers.

key_assumptions.assumption: No confounding from the macroeconomic environment: the effects of the Great Recession and recovery do not vary between job movers and job stayers in a way correlated with the identifying tax variation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stability of the estimates during the recession and recovery, and replication using the 1987 tax reform (Table 3); the authors concede it is difficult to rule out macro effects conclusively.

threats_discussed: Mean reversion: those with high pre-reform incomes tend to be selected on positive transitory shocks, creating downward bias as the shocks dissipate.
Non-tax effects on earnings growth that vary by pre-reform income level, because treatment status is assigned on pre-reform income.
Selection into switching: reform-induced switchers may be selected on the structural elasticity.
The reform may have changed the composition (characteristics) of job switchers even if it barely changed the amount of switching.

Attenuation bias in intention-to-treat estimates as people move across tax brackets after the reform (addressed by instrumenting actual with pre-reform bracket for treatment-on-the-treated estimates).
The 2009 reform coincides with the Great Recession, posing identification threats from heterogeneous effects of the recession and recovery.
robustness_checks: Placebo (pre-reform) estimates using 2006–2008 earnings growth by 2006 income bin.
Quadruple-differences specification netting out the estimate for job stayers.
Dropping all controls, adding demographic controls, and adding demographic controls together with job fixed effects (Table 2 / Table 3, Panel B).
Donut-hole specifications excluding observations within ±2.5 percent and ±5.0 percent of the treatment threshold.
Separate estimates for occupation switches and for firm switches.
Restriction to mass-layoff switchers (Table 2, Table 3, Figure 10).
Bounds on selection bias from tax-induced switching (Figure 9).
Event studies of switcher characteristics (Supplemental Appendix Figure A.6).
Replication of the whole design using the 1987 tax reform (Table 3).
unresolved_confounders: Macroeconomic confounders around the Great Recession: 'it is difficult to rule out macro effects conclusively' (footnote 29, p. 2876).
The switcher elasticity may remain a lower bound, because job movers, while revealing more than job stayers, may still not reveal the full long-run effect (p. 2887).

controls: vector of baseline taxable income bin dummies D_it^Treat (one bin below the treatment threshold omitted)

estimation.clustering: robust standard errors (Table 1 notes, p. 2881)

source_table.value: Table 1, Panel A. Dynamic approach (switchers), two-year elasticity, 2SLS column (p. 2881)

adjustment_set.label: baseline job cell (firm × occupation) fixed effects

mediators_claimed: job switches (transitions between firm × occupation cells), which the paper's model treats as mediating the link between effort/latent earnings and realized earnings

heterogeneity.finding: Job movers feature large responses (an elasticity of about 0.5) while job stayers feature no responses (p. 2852, Figure 6 Panel B).
Switchers in the top decile have even larger elasticities (0.725 after two years, 0.642 after four years; Table 2, Panel A).

ambiguities: The paper prints no p-values or significance stars; statistical significance was read from the ratio of the printed coefficient to the printed robust standard error.

evidence.how: The table prints no significance stars, p-values or confidence intervals. Statistical significance was inferred from the printed coefficient 0.486 and the printed standard error 0.022: |coefficient| / standard error exceeds 1.96, so the estimate is recorded as significant at the 5 percent level. No p-value was computed and none is recorded.

value.lhs: Δlog z_it (log change in total labor compensation)

terms.expression: (β^P′ D_it^Treat × D_it^Mover + γ^P′ D_it^Treat + μ^P D_it^Mover) × D_t^P

value.normalisation: D_i^Treat is a vector of baseline taxable income bin dummies with one bin below the treatment threshold omitted (equation 24); the placebo block is switched on only in the pre-reform period by D_t^P; earnings changes are measured 2008–2010 (two-year) or 2008–2012 (four-year) against the 2006–2008 placebo window.

value.claimed_domain: Long-run earnings elasticities of salaried career workers at the top of the income distribution; the authors state the results are externally valid to a historic Danish tax reform and that extension to other countries is an agenda for future research.

prior_findings_compared.citation: Prescott (2004); Rogerson and Wallenius (2009); Keane and Rogerson (2015) (macro literature)
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: While we argue that the long-run elasticity is larger than typically estimated, our analysis does not support the very large elasticities implied by some macro calibrations.

falsification.condition: The paper states the observable pattern that would overturn point identification of the long-run elasticity from switchers: if structural elasticities and switching probabilities were correlated, the earnings response of switchers would decline (positive correlation) or increase (negative correlation) in the time between the reform and the switch, rather than being constant in the timing of switching (footnote 31, p. 2878).

treatment.label: Δlog(1 − τ_it^sim) — simulated (mechanical) log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate, interacted with the job mover dummy

timing.value: Four-year change from the pre-reform baseline year.

outcome.label: Δlog(1 − τ_it) × D_it^Mover — actual log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate for job movers

definition.value: The actual (realized) log change in the individual's marginal net-of-tax rate interacted with the job mover dummy; this is the endogenous regressor of equation (25) and the dependent variable of the first stage.

units.value: coefficient on the simulated log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate (both sides in log points)

magnitude.interpretation: 'The first stage is extremely strong, with an F-statistic of about 16,000 after two years and 14,000 after four years' (p. 2881).

estimand.formal_query: E[Δlog(1 − τ) × D^Mover | Δlog(1 − τ^sim)] — first-stage relevance

population.description: Danish taxpayers with baseline taxable income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK around the 2009 tax reform, with treatment status assigned by baseline taxable income relative to a threshold at about the seventieth percentile of the income distribution; the elasticity is estimated on job movers (workers switching between firm × occupation cells) relative to job stayers.
subgroups_defined: job movers (switchers between firm × occupation cells) versus job stayers
all switchers versus switchers in the top 10 percent of the income distribution
occupation switches, firm switches, and mass-layoff firm switches
population.selection: Treatment status assigned by baseline (pre-reform) taxable income bin; the estimation sample is restricted to taxpayers with baseline taxable income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK, and the elasticity of interest conditions on making a post-reform firm × occupation switch.

identification.source_of_variation: The 2009–2010 Danish tax reform, which eliminated the middle tax bracket and raised the top-bracket threshold, cutting the marginal tax rate by 11.43 percentage points on average above a treatment threshold located at around the seventieth percentile of the income distribution and by 1.70 percentage points below it (a difference in tax treatment of 9.73 percentage points), combined with variation in job switching between firm × occupation cells.
identification.instrument: Δlog(1 − τ_it^sim), the simulated mechanical change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate holding individual income choices fixed at baseline values (Gruber and Saez 2002)

key_assumptions.assumption: Quadruple-differences assumption: job stayers cannot respond to taxes, so non-tax differences in earnings growth above versus below the treatment threshold may change over time as long as they change in the same way for movers and stayers.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo (pre-reform) estimates are close to zero in the year-by-year profile (Figure 7); the 2006–2008 placebo series tracks the 2008–2010 series below the treatment threshold (Figure 6).

formal.as_written: γ_b − γ_b^P for stayers and β_b + γ_b − (β_b^P + γ_b^P) for movers; preferred estimates based on β_b − β_b^P

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: the simulated mechanical change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate predicts the actual change.
key_assumptions.supported_by: First-stage coefficient 0.486 with F-statistic 16,482.7 (two-year) and 0.441 with F-statistic 14,133.6 (four-year), Table 1 Panel A.

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: the simulated mechanical tax change affects earnings growth only through the actual marginal net-of-tax rate, because it holds individual income choices fixed at baseline values.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the simulated instrument as removing reverse causality from the endogenous choice of earnings in a progressive schedule, but states no separate test of the exclusion restriction.

key_assumptions.assumption: The timing of job switching is not selected on the underlying structural elasticity η (orthogonality between structural elasticities η and switching probabilities λ), which is what allows the switcher elasticity to point identify the long-run elasticity in the population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Flat time profile of mover estimates (Figure 7); bounds on selection bias from tax-induced switching (Figure 9); no effects of the reform on switcher characteristics (Supplemental Appendix Figure A.6); similar responses among mass-layoff switchers (Figure 10 and Table 2).

formal.as_written: E[ε_zt | J_t = 1] = s_t · η^T + (1 − s_t) · η^N

key_assumptions.assumption: Mean reversion: individuals with high pre-reform income are selected on positive transitory shocks, an unobserved common cause of baseline income bin and subsequent earnings growth that the design must net out.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pre-reform (placebo) regressions on 2006–2008 earnings growth by 2006 income bin; the quadruple-differences specification nets out stayers.

key_assumptions.assumption: No confounding from the macroeconomic environment: the effects of the Great Recession and recovery do not vary between job movers and job stayers in a way correlated with the identifying tax variation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stability of the estimates during the recession and recovery, and replication using the 1987 tax reform (Table 3); the authors concede it is difficult to rule out macro effects conclusively.

threats_discussed: Mean reversion: those with high pre-reform incomes tend to be selected on positive transitory shocks, creating downward bias as the shocks dissipate.
Non-tax effects on earnings growth that vary by pre-reform income level, because treatment status is assigned on pre-reform income.
Selection into switching: reform-induced switchers may be selected on the structural elasticity.
The reform may have changed the composition (characteristics) of job switchers even if it barely changed the amount of switching.

Attenuation bias in intention-to-treat estimates as people move across tax brackets after the reform (addressed by instrumenting actual with pre-reform bracket for treatment-on-the-treated estimates).
The 2009 reform coincides with the Great Recession, posing identification threats from heterogeneous effects of the recession and recovery.
robustness_checks: Placebo (pre-reform) estimates using 2006–2008 earnings growth by 2006 income bin.
Quadruple-differences specification netting out the estimate for job stayers.
Dropping all controls, adding demographic controls, and adding demographic controls together with job fixed effects (Table 2 / Table 3, Panel B).
Donut-hole specifications excluding observations within ±2.5 percent and ±5.0 percent of the treatment threshold.
Separate estimates for occupation switches and for firm switches.
Restriction to mass-layoff switchers (Table 2, Table 3, Figure 10).
Bounds on selection bias from tax-induced switching (Figure 9).
Event studies of switcher characteristics (Supplemental Appendix Figure A.6).
Replication of the whole design using the 1987 tax reform (Table 3).
unresolved_confounders: Macroeconomic confounders around the Great Recession: 'it is difficult to rule out macro effects conclusively' (footnote 29, p. 2876).
The switcher elasticity may remain a lower bound, because job movers, while revealing more than job stayers, may still not reveal the full long-run effect (p. 2887).

definition.value: Dummy (or vector of baseline taxable income bin dummies) equal to one if the individual's baseline, pre-reform taxable income is above the threshold at which the 1987 Danish tax reform cut the marginal tax rate. The measure of taxable income that determines treatment status includes labor income, transfers, pensions, alimony, and certain capital income items.

timing.value: Assigned on pre-reform (baseline) taxable income; effects measured two and four years after the reform.

outcome.label: D_it^Mover — probability of switching jobs

definition.value: Dummy equal to one if individual i made a job switch (any switch between firm × occupation cells) between the base year and year t; the two- and four-year effects are cumulative switching probabilities over those windows. Switches are dropped where more than 50 percent of an individual's coworkers move to the same job cell in the same year.

timing.value: Cumulative probability of a post-reform switch by two and by four years after the reform.

units.value: change in the probability of making a job switch (probability units, 0–1)

estimand.target_population: workers treated by the 1987 reform (baseline income above the treatment threshold), under the baseline specification on all switchers
estimand.time_horizon: four-year effect around the 1987 tax reform (exact calendar windows not printed)
estimand.formal_query: E[D^Mover | do(treated by the reform)] − E[D^Mover | do(untreated)] (equation 26)

population.description: Danish taxpayers around the 1987 tax reform, which reduced marginal tax rates at the top of the distribution relative to rates further down; the table is constructed in the exact same way as the 2009-reform tables, so the sample is taxpayers in the baseline income window who switch between firm × occupation cells.
population.period: around the 1987 Danish tax reform (exact estimation windows not printed in the paper)
subgroups_defined: all switchers versus top 10 percent switchers
occupation switches, firm switches, and mass-layoff firm switches
population.selection: Treatment status assigned by baseline (pre-reform) taxable income relative to the threshold changed by the 1987 reform; the elasticity conditions on making a post-reform job switch.

identification.source_of_variation: The 1987 Danish tax reform, which, like the 2009 reform, reduced tax rates at the top of the distribution relative to tax rates further down; only this reform among the four pre-2009 Danish reforms significantly changed the taxation of top earners relative to bottom and middle earners.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the reform, the switching probabilities of the treatment and control groups would have evolved in the same way.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The pre-reform coefficients β̂_t of equation (26) are used to assess the assumption; Figure 8 shows parallel trends in the switching probabilities of treatment and control groups before the reform.

formal.as_written: Equation (26) is a standard event study specification in which the parallel-trend assumption can be assessed based on the estimated coefficients β̂_t in the pre-reform years

key_assumptions.assumption: No non-tax effects on the probability of switching that vary by pre-reform income level, since treatment status is assigned on pre-reform income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states this threat for the earnings-growth outcome and relies on pre-reform event-study coefficients for the switching outcome.

threats_discussed: Mean reversion: those with high pre-reform incomes tend to be selected on positive transitory shocks, creating downward bias as the shocks dissipate.
Non-tax effects on earnings growth that vary by pre-reform income level, because treatment status is assigned on pre-reform income.
Selection into switching: reform-induced switchers may be selected on the structural elasticity.
The reform may have changed the composition (characteristics) of job switchers even if it barely changed the amount of switching.

Attenuation bias in intention-to-treat estimates as people move across tax brackets after the reform (addressed by instrumenting actual with pre-reform bracket for treatment-on-the-treated estimates).
robustness_checks: Placebo (pre-reform) estimates using 2006–2008 earnings growth by 2006 income bin.
Quadruple-differences specification netting out the estimate for job stayers.
Dropping all controls, adding demographic controls, and adding demographic controls together with job fixed effects (Table 2 / Table 3, Panel B).
Donut-hole specifications excluding observations within ±2.5 percent and ±5.0 percent of the treatment threshold.
Separate estimates for occupation switches and for firm switches.
Restriction to mass-layoff switchers (Table 2, Table 3, Figure 10).
Bounds on selection bias from tax-induced switching (Figure 9).
Event studies of switcher characteristics (Supplemental Appendix Figure A.6).
Replication of the whole design using the 1987 tax reform (Table 3).
unresolved_confounders: The switcher elasticity may remain a lower bound, because job movers, while revealing more than job stayers, may still not reveal the full long-run effect (p. 2887).

estimation.specification: Equation (26), difference-in-differences / event-study specification for the switching probability; the baseline specification on all switchers
estimation.clustering: not stated in the Table 2 / Table 3 notes; Table 1, which reports the same baseline specification, states robust standard errors (p. 2881)

source_table.value: Table 3, Panel A. Baseline specification, row 'All switchers', column 'Probability of switching: Four-year effect' (p. 2886)

ambiguities: The table prints no p-values or significance stars; statistical significance was read from the ratio of the printed coefficient to the printed standard error.

evidence.how: The table prints no significance stars, p-values or confidence intervals. Statistical significance was inferred from the printed coefficient 0.018 and the printed standard error 0.002: |coefficient| / standard error exceeds 1.96, so the estimate is recorded as significant at the 5 percent level. key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the simulated instrument as removing reverse causality from the endogenous choice of earnings in a progressive schedule, but states no separate test of the exclusion restriction.

claims.statement: For the full population of treated workers, the 2009 tax reform raised earnings: reducing the top marginal tax rate by about 10 percentage points increased earnings by less than 2 percent.

treatment.label: Treated by the 2009 tax reform (baseline taxable income above the treatment threshold)

definition.value: Vector of baseline taxable income bin dummies D_i^Treat, omitting a bin below the treatment threshold; the threshold separating treatments and controls was located at around the seventieth percentile of the income distribution. The reform reduced the marginal tax rate above the threshold by 11.43 percentage points on average and below it by 1.70 percentage points.

timing.value: Assigned on 2008 (pre-reform) taxable income for the reform window and on 2006 income for the placebo window.

outcome.label: Delta log earnings - two-year change in log earnings

definition.value: Change in log earnings between 2008 and 2010 (reform period), compared with the change between 2006 and 2008 (pre-reform, placebo period), by baseline taxable income bin. z_i is total labor compensation including contributions to employer-administrated retirement savings plans.

timing.value: Two-year change from the 2008 baseline, against the 2006-2008 placebo window.

units.value: percent increase in earnings from a reduction of the top marginal tax rate by about 10 percentage points

magnitude.interpretation: 'The effect is visually clear and precisely estimated, but modest in size. Reducing the top marginal tax rate by about 10 percentage points increases earnings by less than 2 percent' (p. 2876).

estimand.target_population: all treated Danish workers (baseline taxable income above the treatment threshold), regardless of job switching status
estimand.time_horizon: two-year change, 2008-2010, relative to the 2006-2008 placebo window
estimand.formal_query: gamma_b - gamma_b^P: triple-differences effect of the reform on the two-year log earnings change, by baseline income bin

population.description: All Danish workers around the 2009 tax reform, binned by baseline taxable income from about 200,000 to 800,000 DKK, with treatment status set by position relative to the threshold.
subgroups_defined: treated (above threshold) versus control (below threshold) income bins
population.selection: Treatment status assigned by baseline (pre-reform) taxable income bin; the estimation sample is restricted to taxpayers with baseline taxable income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK, and the elasticity of interest conditions on making a post-reform firm × occupation switch.

identification.source_of_variation: The 2009–2010 Danish tax reform, which eliminated the middle tax bracket and raised the top-bracket threshold, cutting the marginal tax rate by 11.43 percentage points on average above a treatment threshold located at around the seventieth percentile of the income distribution and by 1.70 percentage points below it (a difference in tax treatment of 9.73 percentage points), combined with variation in job switching between firm × occupation cells.

key_assumptions.assumption: Non-tax differences in earnings growth above versus below the treatment threshold (notably mean reversion) are stable over time, so the pre-reform (2006-2008) difference-in-differences identifies them and can be netted out.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The 2008-2010 and 2006-2008 series track each other almost perfectly below the treatment threshold, which the paper reads as mean reversion being stable over time.

formal.as_written: gamma_b - gamma_b^P for stayers and beta_b + gamma_b - (beta_b^P + gamma_b^P) for movers

key_assumptions.assumption: Mean reversion: individuals with high pre-reform income are selected on positive transitory shocks, an unobserved common cause of baseline income bin and subsequent earnings growth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The pre-reform placebo series shows the same negative relationship between earnings growth and baseline income.

key_assumptions.assumption: No non-tax effects on the probability of switching that vary by pre-reform income level, since treatment status is assigned on pre-reform income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper relies on the pre-reform event-study coefficients.

threats_discussed: Mean reversion: those with high pre-reform incomes tend to be selected on positive transitory shocks, creating downward bias as the shocks dissipate.
Non-tax effects on earnings growth that vary by pre-reform income level, because treatment status is assigned on pre-reform income.

claims.statement: Selection bias from tax-induced job switching is quantitatively unimportant: even assuming elasticities as high as four for tax-induced movers, the implied population-wide elasticity stays close to the estimated switcher elasticity.

treatment.label: Assumed structural elasticity of tax-induced movers (eta^T)

definition.value: The assumed structural elasticity for workers who switch jobs because of the reform, varied along the x-axis from 0 to 4 ('well beyond the conceivable range'). timing.value: Based on the four-year estimates of the earnings elasticity and of the effect on job-switching probability.

outcome.label: Implied true long-run earnings elasticity in the full population

timing.value: Four-year horizon.

units.value: elasticity units: the vertical gap between the estimated elasticity (black line) and the implied true elasticity (red line) in the figure

population.description: Danish taxpayers with baseline taxable income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK around the 2009 tax reform, with treatment status assigned by baseline taxable income relative to a threshold at about the seventieth percentile of the income distribution; the elasticity is estimated on job movers (workers switching between firm × occupation cells) relative to job stayers.

threats_discussed: Mean reversion: those with high pre-reform incomes tend to be selected on positive transitory shocks, creating downward bias as the shocks dissipate.
